title: Trump Says Russia Has 'Lost Control' of Its Oil Industry, Plans to Confront Zelensky Over Refinery Strikes at NYC Meeting
subhead: With the US president publicly criticizing Moscow on energy for the first time, refinery strikes on both the Russian and Iranian supply lines are now the dominant driver of global oil prices, alongside a diesel shortage expected to last into 2027.

sections.heading: Trump Turns on Moscow Over Refinery Strikes
sections.body: US President Donald Trump has said Russia has 'lost control' of its oil industry, a rare public criticism of Moscow, ahead of an Oval Office-adjacent meeting with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in New York this week. According to reports cited by The Gateway Pundit and The Chronicle, Trump plans to confront Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, which have tightened global fuel supply and pushed prices to painful levels. Zelensky is set to travel to New York to meet the US president, with refinery strikes high on the agenda — a shift from Washington's earlier stance toward the campaign that has taken out Russian processing capacity.
sections.whyItMatters: It signals a hardening US position that Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure — not just Iranian supply — are now seen by the White House as a price problem Washington must address, putting energy policy at the center of US-Ukraine diplomacy.

sections.heading: Global Diesel Shortage Set to Last Into 2027
sections.body: A global diesel shortage fueled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine is unlikely to ease before next year, Reuters reports, citing storage market indicators and industry participants. Stockpiles have drained to record lows as wars knocked out exports from top producers including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Diesel prices have hit record highs in both Europe and the United States, with market watchers warning the tightness leaves little room to absorb further disruptions. Storage and inventory indicators point to a shortage that extends into 2027, weighing on freight, farming, and industrial economies worldwide.
sections.whyItMatters: Diesel is the workhorse fuel of the global economy; a shortage this persistent pushes up the cost of moving everything, sharpening the economic pain of both wars and raising the political stakes for any ceasefire that does not restore refining capacity.

sections.heading: Oil Slips a Fourth Day as Hormuz Flows Improve
sections.body: Brent crude fell 1.7% to $102.08 a barrel on Monday, extending a fourth consecutive session of declines, as improving flows through the Strait of Hormuz and renewed prospects for diplomacy over the Iran conflict eased immediate supply concerns, per Pakistan Today's market coverage. The two conflicts dominating energy markets — Iran and Ukraine — are settling into a 'grim and costly stalemate' with no sign of a breakthrough, Reuters commentary notes. The daily retreat marks a modest easing from the crisis highs, but prices remain far above pre-war levels.
sections.whyItMatters: The slide shows markets are pricing in partial supply restoration — or at least the absence of escalation — through Hormuz, but the underlying structural deficit in refined products remains, keeping price downside limited.

sections.heading: India's Coal Crisis: 74 Plants Critically Low
sections.body: Nearly 40% of India's coal-fired power plants are running with critically low fuel stocks, government data show, as electricity demand rises amid hotter El Niño-linked weather. Coal inventories at thermal plants fell to 22.9 million tonnes on September 19 — just 39% of normative stock — with 74 of 190 plants flagged as critical, Business Standard reports. Reuters adds that India's coal demand is set to jump 4.2%, while transport bottlenecks are straining deliveries. The crunch comes even as a surge of solar capacity has arguably kept the shortfall from being worse.
sections.whyItMatters: For Asia's third-largest economy, a coal stockout risks rolling power cuts just as the diesel and LNG squeeze bites; it also underscores how India's energy security rests on a strained domestic logistics chain more than on imported fuel.

sections.heading: Asian LNG Demand Falls Second Year as War Shrinks Gulf Supply
sections.body: Asian demand for liquefied natural gas is on track to decline for a second consecutive year, Reuters reports, as the war on Iran curtails Gulf exports, tightening availability and lifting prices to multi-year highs that cut consumption. In a parallel move, LNG buyers and sellers are actively seeking greater supply diversity to hedge against Gulf disruption, per a Reuters dispatch from Bangkok. The combination means Asia — the world's largest LNG import market — is consuming less this year while paying more, a demand-destruction pattern that mirrors the 2022 energy crisis.
sections.whyItMatters: Persistent Gulf supply loss is pushing Asian buyers to lock in alternative sources and rethink long-term contracts, reshaping the LNG trade map and strengthening the negotiating hand of non-Gulf exporters.

sections.heading: Houthis Push to Cut Off Yemen's Red Sea Coast
sections.body: Houthi fighters are pushing to seize strategic mountain positions in Yemen to isolate the country's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government forces, according to The Vibes, citing Reuters. The escalation in ground fighting comes alongside continued Houthi missile and drone pressure on Saudi oil facilities, which Reuters notes has slowed ship traffic through Bab el-Mandeb. Control over the Yemeni Red Sea littoral would deepen the Houthis' ability to threaten the shipping lane that connects the Suez route to the Indian Ocean.
sections.whyItMatters: Though overshadowed by the Iran and Ukraine fronts, the Houthi push to consolidate the Red Sea coastline keeps a key global chokepoint under active threat and complicates any Red Sea shipping normalization.

bottomLine: The day's story is the re-centering of energy policy inside the Russia-Ukraine war: Trump's public line that Moscow has 'lost control' of its oil industry and his plan to confront Zelensky over refinery strikes make Russian processing capacity — not just Iranian supply — a top-tier driver of global prices. Beneath that, a diesel shortage set to run into 2027, record fuel costs, India's coal crunch, and shrinking Asian LNG demand show the economic strain of both conflicts spreading well beyond the battlefields. A fourth-day retreat in Brent to $102 offers only modest relief while refined-product deficits persist.
sources: Reuters, The Gateway Pundit, The Chronicle, Pakistan Today, Business Standard, Firstpost, Dawn, The Vibes (via Reuters), OilPrice.com
